title: AIIMS' Homegrown AI for Breast Cancer Detection Moves Toward Hospitals
excerpt: AIIMS Delhi has transferred its mammography AI — trained entirely on Indian data — to BPL Technologies for regulatory approval and hospital deployment.
body:
• Doctors and researchers at AIIMS Delhi have developed an artificial intelligence tool that acts as a second reader of mammograms, flagging possible signs of breast cancer for radiologists.
  • On September 16, AIIMS transferred the technology to BPL Technologies Ltd for further development, regulatory approval and deployment in hospitals across India.
  • The model was trained entirely on Indian patient data — described as the first Indian version of a mammography AI — and showed a 99% negative predictive value in retrospective testing on 3,000 to 4,000 patients.
  • The tool has run in trial mode at AIIMS for about a year without making clinical decisions; BPL says it could reach hospitals in around six months, depending on regulatory clearances.

A Second Pair of Eyes

An artificial intelligence tool developed by doctors and researchers at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences in Delhi can act as a second reader of mammograms — scanning the images and alerting radiologists to possible signs of breast cancer they might otherwise miss.

On Wednesday, September 16, AIIMS transferred the technology to Indian healthcare technology company BPL Technologies Ltd, which will take the model through further development, regulatory approval and deployment in hospitals. The handover marks the step from research project to potential clinical product.

Dr Krithika Rangarajan, Associate Professor in the Department of Diagnostic and Interventional Oncoradiology at AIIMS, said the model was designed as a safety net. "The idea is to act as a second reader and alert the radiologist to any possible cancer, so that they do not miss cancers on mammography," she said. It is aimed particularly at hospitals where doctors have limited experience interpreting mammograms or where breast imaging specialists are in short supply — a common situation outside India's metro hospitals.

Trained on Indian Data

What sets the model apart, according to Rangarajan, is its training data: it was built entirely on Indian patient data, making it the first Indian version of a mammography AI model. Most commercial imaging AI is trained on Western datasets, which do not always generalise well to Indian patients.

Developed over roughly one to one-and-a-half years with initial funding from the Ministry of Education, the model was retrospectively tested on around 3,000 to 4,000 patients at AIIMS. At the threshold used in the study, it showed a 99% negative predictive value — meaning that when the model indicated no cancer, it was correct about 99% of the time in that study setting. Performance, researchers caution, depends on the threshold chosen and the clinical setting.

The system has been running at AIIMS in trial mode for around a year. It is not being used to make clinical decisions: patients continue to receive reports from radiologists while researchers separately assess what the AI flags.

The Global Context

The AIIMS work arrives as evidence for AI-assisted mammography builds worldwide. In Sweden's national breast cancer screening programme, a study of more than 105,900 women found that AI-supported mammography reduced interval cancers — malignancies detected between scheduled screenings — by 12% compared with standard double reading by radiologists, while detecting 9% more cancers at screening, with similar false-positive rates.

Breast cancer has overtaken cervical cancer as the most common cancer among Indian women in urban areas, and late detection remains a major driver of mortality. A reliable second reader could matter most precisely where radiology expertise is thinnest.

"The idea is to act as a second reader and alert the radiologist to any possible cancer, so that they do not miss cancers on mammography."

— Dr Krithika Rangarajan, AIIMS Delhi

What Comes Next

BPL Technologies will now convert the research model into a finished product, conduct further validation, obtain regulatory clearances and provide technical support for hospital deployment. Rangarajan said the tool could potentially reach hospitals in around six months, depending on how quickly approvals come through.

The path from promising retrospective numbers to a regulated clinical device is where many medical AI projects stall. If BPL clears it, India would have a homegrown screening aid built on its own population's data — and a template for how public research hospitals can move AI from the lab to the ward.
